episodes.189026: A cold front dropped southward across Central Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours of April 14, 2024, accompanied by a line of showers and storms. The storms developed in a relatively dry environment, with plentiful shear and adequate CAPE. Damaging winds were the primary issue, although there were two reports of quarter-sized hail. The storms weakened as they moved into southern Pennsylvania late in the evening.
episodes.189027: Scattered showers and storms developed in the vicinity of a lingering frontal boundary near the Mason-Dixon line during the afternoon of April 15, 2024. One particularly strong storm produced up to ping pong ball sized hail and wind damage in Adams and York Counties.
episodes.189043: A powerful upper level storm system tracked across the central Rocky Mountains on the 15th. A strong surface cyclone developed in eastern Colorado out ahead of this system also producing a compact dryline. This dryline started out in the western South Plains in the morning and moved eastward through the day tightening its dew point gradient along the way. Ample instability existed east of the dryline along with sufficient deep layer wind shear to produce severe storms. However, cloud cover prevented convective initiation for much of the afternoon. Once clouds cleared out late in the afternoon, thunderstorms quickly developed and became severe. One severe storm produced hail up to quarter size as it tracked to the northeast across Stonewall County. Later in the evening, a pacific cold front rushed through the area. Strong westerly winds in the wake of the front produced a severe wind gust of 59 mph near Roaring Springs measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet.

episodes.189731: A line of convection developed along passing cold front and trough during the late afternoon of April 14th over Lake Erie. The line matured and slowly progressed south and created severe hail and flooding due to training. Effective shear was maximized between 18Z and 00Z over northern PA with a low-level jet originated from west to east.  Surface instability likely ranged from 500J/kg to 1000J/kg and shear from the surface to 500mb likely ranged between 45kt to 55kts.
episodes.189733: Early afternoon convection developed along a slow moving frontal boundary in northern West Virginia. An isolated storm had severe hail observed due to high effective wind shear (+40kts) and instability ranging between 750J/kg to 1500J/kg.
episodes.189820: At the surface, a low moved southeastward from western Lake Ontario to near Long Island Sound during the early afternoon through late evening of the 14th. Simultaneously, the trailing cold front swept southward from southern portions of ON, MI, and Lake Michigan, respectively, to central portions of IN, OH, and PA, respectively. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward or southeastward across northeast OH during the late afternoon through early evening. The storms produced hail, some of which was severe, in several counties, and a severe peak convective wind gust in Trumbull County. The storms' ambient environment exhibited weak to moderate MUCAPE, steep midlevel lapse rates near 7C-8C/km, moderate DCAPE, and moderate to strong effective bulk shear.
episodes.189973: A warm frontal boundary lifted across central and north central Nebraska during the late afternoon and evening hours of April 15th. With afternoon heating and the frontal boundary, thunderstorms developed along a broken line from Cody to Tryon. As this activity lifted northeast, it became severe with hail up to golf ball size in northern Cherry County.
episodes.190006: A stalled front over northern Delaware resulted in the development of isolated strong to severe thunderstorms. One storm produced damaging wind gusts in the northern portion of the state.
episodes.190082: Active weather took place each afternoon in West Virginia from April 15th to the 17th in the midst of a slow moving upper level disturbance. Isolated to scattered thunderstorms resulted in instances of downed trees and power lines from damaging wind gusts and hail stones ranging from nickel size to golf ball size. Storms were primarily driven by daytime heating, weakening in intensity each evening after sunset.
episodes.190565: After several days of heavy rain from thunderstorms across the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic region, water drained down the Ohio River. During the early morning hours of April 15th, the river gauge at Ashland denoted a rise above flood stage and remained the case until later that evening. This resulted in minor flooding in the Catlettsburg area during that time.
episodes.190929: A closed low over the Central Rockies with an attendant jet streak resulted in localized high winds across southeast New Mexico. Further east, severe thunderstorms developed ahead of the dryline. Lastly, a localized heat burst and high winds occurred near the Delaware Mountains.
episodes.191071: Slow moving thunderstorm brought heavy rain the area. Rain gages in the area were spotty but had storm total of 1.9 to 2.5 inches between 7 and 10 pm PDT. Radar estimated around half an inch of rain in the area.
episodes.191090: Under a surface-induced perturbation and associated mid to upper-level through...an unsettled workweek was observed for most of the region. Above normal precipitable water (PWAT) values was observed, with available moisture reaching the mid to upper levels. All of this caused the potential for isolated to scattered thunderstorms to increase. Although PWAT values decreased on Wednesday, fairly unstable conditions, diurnal and local effects promoted continued convective development for the second half of the workweek under ENE winds. This weather pattern lead to quick river rises and water surges with flooding, flash flooding, and landslides.
episodes.191224: Scattered severe thunderstorms in advance of a cold front produced damaging winds and large hail across portions of central and eastern Virginia.
episodes.191225: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a cold front produced gusty winds across portions of the Chesapeake Bay and Virginia Coastal Waters.

Slow moving thunderstorms produced 1 to 2 inches of rain over 3 hours on Highway 162 just southwest of Kamiah. Flash flooding occurred along Fort Misery Road just south of Highway 162 with 1.5 to 2 miles of roadway destroyed. Debris from Fort Misery Road washed on to Highway 162 with the highway closed around 12 hours. One car was caught in the debris flow but no injuries were reported. Also, one power pole was lost in the debris slide causing 8 customers to lose power. Seven Mile Creek came out of its banks, and began forming a new channel just upstream from its confluence with Lawyer Creek. Water and some debris also washed over Highway 12 in several places between mile markers 63 to 66 (mostly Lewis County) requiring brief mitigation.
Emergency manager reported debris flow over Highway 64. It closed the section of road between milepost 23 to 31.  Cost of repair is estimated.

The Ohio River at Ashland rose above flood stage shortly after midnight on the 15th of April. The river continued to rise to a crest of around 52 feet later that morning and then eased back below flood stage that evening. Minor flooding of roads in low lying areas near Catlettsburg occurred during the time the Ohio River was above its flood stage.
